topics.title: GST Payment Framework and Types of E-Ledgers
explain: Under GST, every registered person gets three electronic ledgers on the common portal dashboard.
Electronic Cash Ledger acts like a digital wallet reflecting all cash deposits and tax deductions.
Electronic Credit Ledger holds self-assessed input tax credit claimed through monthly returns.
Electronic Liability Register records all tax, interest, late fees, and penalty liabilities due.
Intra-State supplies require CGST and SGST/UTGST, while inter-State supplies require IGST.

flow.title: Functioning of the Three GST Ledgers
steps: Register on GST Common Portal
Access three auto-created ledgers
Deposit cash or record ITC
Discharge liabilities reflected in register

topics.example: When Mohan logs into GST portal, he sees his cash balance in cash ledger, input tax in credit ledger, and monthly tax due in liability register.
remember: Cash and Credit ledgers are updated by taxpayer deposits and claims, while Liability Register tracks government dues.
mistakes: Thinking that the Electronic Liability Register is maintained manually by the taxpayer instead of being auto-updated on the portal.

quiz.q: Which of the following registers is maintained on the GST portal to record the tax liabilities of a taxpayer?
quiz.why: Section 49(7) provides that all liabilities of a taxable person shall be recorded in the Electronic Liability Register.

quiz.q: Which two e-ledgers are prepared and updated based on deposits and return claims of the taxpayer?
o: Electronic Liability Register and Cash Ledger
Electronic Cash Ledger and Credit Ledger
Electronic Credit Ledger and Audit Register
Electronic Liability Register and Credit Ledger
quiz.why: Electronic Cash Ledger and Electronic Credit Ledger are updated by the taxpayer's own deposits and self-assessed ITC claims.

topics.title: Electronic Cash Ledger and Challan Rules
explain: Cash can be deposited via Internet Banking, UPI, IMPS, Cards, NEFT/RTGS, or Over-the-Counter (OTC).
Over-the-Counter payments in cash, cheque, or DD are capped at ₹10,000 per challan per tax period.
The ₹10,000 OTC limit does not apply to Government departments, recovery officers, or enforcement deposits.
Form GST PMT-06 generates an e-challan with a 14-digit CPIN valid for 15 days.
On successful bank payment, a 17-digit CIN (CPIN + 3-digit bank code) is generated and credited to the cash ledger.
If payment succeeds but CIN is not generated or updated, file a representation in Form GST PMT-07.

flow.title: Deposit Process into Electronic Cash Ledger
steps: Generate challan in Form GST PMT-06
Obtain 14-digit CPIN valid 15 days
Pay online or submit bank mandate
Bank generates 17-digit CIN
Cash ledger credited automatically

topics.example: Ajay generates a challan for ₹8,000 on 1st October; he must complete the OTC payment at his bank by 16th October before the CPIN expires.
remember: CPIN is 14 digits and valid for 15 days; CIN is 17 digits; OTC payment limit is ₹10,000 per challan per tax period.
mistakes: Believing physical or manual paper challans can be filled at the bank without generating Form GST PMT-06 online.

quiz.q: What is the maximum limit for Over the Counter (OTC) cash deposit per challan per tax period?
quiz.why: Rule 87 restricts OTC payments to ₹10,000 per challan per tax period, subject to specific official exceptions.

quiz.q: What is the validity period of an e-challan generated in Form GST PMT-06?
quiz.why: A challan generated on the GST portal remains valid for 15 days from the date of generation.

topics.title: Heads of Account and Transfer of Cash Ledger Balance
explain: The Electronic Cash Ledger has 4 Major Heads (IGST, CGST, SGST/UTGST, Cess).
Each Major Head is divided into 5 Minor Heads: Tax, Interest, Penalty, Fee, and Others.
Taxpayers can transfer unutilized cash between any major/minor heads using Form GST PMT-09.
Funds in the cash ledger can also be transferred to the CGST/IGST cash ledger of a distinct person.
Transfer to a distinct person is strictly barred if the registered person has any unpaid liability.

flow.title: Transfer of Cash Balance via Form GST PMT-09
steps: Check unutilized cash in cash ledger
Confirm absence of unpaid liabilities
File Form GST PMT-09 online
Reallocate funds across heads or distinct person

topics.example: Kavita accidentally deposits ₹4,000 under CGST-Interest instead of CGST-Tax; she shifts it to CGST-Tax using Form GST PMT-09.
remember: Form GST PMT-09 is used to transfer cash balance across heads or to distinct persons without applying for a refund.
mistakes: Assuming cash lying under 'Fee' can automatically offset a 'Tax' liability without filing Form GST PMT-09.

quiz.q: Which form is used to transfer amounts across major or minor heads in the Electronic Cash Ledger?
quiz.why: Form GST PMT-09 is the prescribed form for intra-head or inter-head transfers of cash ledger balances.

quiz.q: Transfer of cash ledger balance to a distinct person's cash ledger is prohibited when:
o: The taxpayer has turnover below ₹1 crore
The taxpayer has any unpaid liability in liability register
The recipient operates in the same State
quiz.why: Section 49(10) proviso states no transfer to a distinct person is allowed if there is any unpaid liability in the electronic liability register.

topics.title: Electronic Credit Ledger and Utilization of ITC
explain: Self-assessed ITC reported in returns is credited to the Electronic Credit Ledger.
Credit ledger balances can ONLY be used to pay output tax under the CGST or IGST Act.
ITC can never be used to pay interest, penalty, late fees, or reverse charge mechanism (RCM) tax.
IGST credit must be fully exhausted first against IGST, then CGST/SGST/UTGST in any order or proportion.
CGST credit is used for CGST first, then IGST; it can NEVER be cross-utilized for SGST/UTGST.
SGST/UTGST credit is used for SGST/UTGST first, then IGST (only when CGST credit is exhausted); never for CGST.

flow.title: Order of ITC Utilization
steps: Exhaust IGST credit against IGST liability
Use remaining IGST for CGST/SGST freely
Use CGST credit for CGST, then IGST
Use SGST credit for SGST, then IGST
Never cross-utilize CGST and SGST

topics.example: Rohit has an RCM tax liability of ₹3,000 on GTA services; he cannot use his ₹10,000 credit ledger balance and must pay ₹3,000 through the cash ledger.
remember: ITC can only pay output tax; RCM liability is not output tax and must be paid in cash.
mistakes: Attempting to set off CGST credit against SGST liability or vice versa, which is legally barred.

quiz.q: Can balance in the Electronic Credit Ledger be used to pay tax payable under Reverse Charge Mechanism (RCM)?
o: No, RCM must be paid through cash ledger
Yes, if sanctioned by the proper officer
quiz.why: Output tax excludes tax payable on reverse charge basis under Section 2(82), so RCM must be discharged via cash ledger.

quiz.q: Which credit must be fully exhausted before utilizing CGST or SGST credit?
quiz.why: Section 49A mandates that ITC on account of IGST must be utilized completely before using CGST or SGST credits.

topics.title: Restrictions on Electronic Credit Ledger Usage
explain: Rule 86A empowers an officer not below Assistant Commissioner to block fraudulent or ineligible ITC.
Reasons for blocking ITC from being used for tax payment or refund must be recorded in writing.
Rule 86B restricts credit ledger usage to 99% of output tax liability for certain high-turnover taxpayers.
This 99% restriction applies when monthly taxable supply value (excluding exempt and zero-rated supplies) exceeds ₹50 lakh.
Affected taxpayers must mandatorily discharge at least 1% of their output tax liability in cash.

flow.title: Applying Rule 86B Payment Restriction
steps: Check monthly taxable supplies exceed ₹50 lakh
Calculate gross output tax liability
Discharge maximum 99% using credit ledger
Pay minimum 1% through cash ledger

topics.example: Apex Traders sells taxable goods worth ₹80 lakh in October with a GST liability of ₹2,00,000; it can pay at most ₹1,98,000 via ITC and must pay ₹2,000 in cash.
remember: Rule 86B requires a minimum 1% cash payment when monthly taxable supplies exceed ₹50 lakh.
mistakes: Applying the 1% cash payment rule to all taxpayers regardless of whether their monthly taxable turnover crosses ₹50 lakh.

quiz.q: Under Rule 86B, what maximum percentage of output tax liability can be discharged through the Electronic Credit Ledger by specified taxpayers?
quiz.why: Rule 86B caps the utilization of Electronic Credit Ledger to 99% of output tax liability, requiring at least 1% in cash.

quiz.q: What is the threshold of taxable supply value per month to trigger the restrictions under Rule 86B?
quiz.why: Rule 86B applies where the value of taxable supplies other than exempt and zero-rated supplies exceeds ₹50 lakh in a month.

topics.title: Electronic Liability Register and Order of Discharge
explain: All tax dues, interest, penalties, and demand amounts are tracked in the Electronic Liability Register.
Taxpayers must follow a strict statutory sequence to clear their liabilities.
Step 1: Self-assessed tax and other dues relating to returns of previous tax periods.
Step 2: Self-assessed tax and other dues relating to returns of the current tax period.
Step 3: Other dues determined under section 73, section 74, or section 74A (demand proceedings).
Section 49(9) presumes every taxable person has passed on the full tax incidence to the recipient.

flow.title: Statutory Order of Discharging Dues
steps: Clear previous periods return dues first
Clear current period return dues next
Clear demand under section 73/74/74A last

topics.example: A firm has an unfiled GSTR-3B from June, its July return, and an audit demand notice; it must clear June dues first, then July, and the demand notice last.
remember: Chronological order: Previous return dues → Current return dues → Adjudication demands under Sec 73/74/74A.
mistakes: Discharging current month dues before clearing self-assessed taxes of previous tax periods.

quiz.q: Which liability must be discharged first according to Section 49(8)?
o: Self-assessed dues of the current tax period
Self-assessed dues of previous tax periods
Penalty for the current tax period
quiz.why: Under Section 49(8)(a), dues related to returns of previous tax periods must be discharged first.

quiz.q: Under the CGST Act, demand notices under Section 73, 74, or 74A are discharged at which stage?
o: Prior to previous tax period dues
Last, after clearing previous and current return dues
quiz.why: Demand liabilities arising from adjudication proceedings come last under Section 49(8)(c).

topics.title: Interest on Delayed Payment of Tax
explain: Default or delay in paying tax attracts interest not exceeding 18% p.a. (notified rate is 18% per annum).
Interest accrues automatically from the day following the payment due date up to the actual payment date.
For returns filed belatedly, interest applies ONLY to the net tax liability paid through Electronic Cash Ledger.
However, if return was filed on time but tax was short-paid, interest applies to the gross unpaid tax amount.
Cash balance deposited into cash ledger on or before due date and used for return filing does not attract interest.

flow.title: Interest Calculation on Belated Return Filing
steps: Determine the delay period from due date
Identify net tax paid via cash ledger
Exclude tax paid via credit ledger
Apply 18% p.a. interest on cash portion

topics.example: Sunil files his return 30 days late, paying ₹20,000 via cash ledger and ₹50,000 via credit ledger; interest is calculated only on ₹20,000 at 18% p.a. for 30 days.
remember: Interest rate for delayed tax payment is 18% per annum, calculated on net cash liability when return is filed late.
mistakes: Computing interest on gross tax liability when a return is filed late before demand proceedings begin.

quiz.q: What is the notified rate of interest per annum under Section 50(1) for belated payment of tax?
quiz.why: Notification No. 13/2017 CT specifies the interest rate as 18% per annum for delayed tax payment.

quiz.q: When a return under Section 39 is filed after the due date, interest under Section 50(1) is calculated on:
o: Portion paid by debiting electronic cash ledger
Portion paid by debiting electronic credit ledger
Total turnover of the tax period
quiz.why: The proviso to Section 50(1) clarifies that interest is levied only on the net tax paid via the electronic cash ledger.

topics.title: Interest on Wrongly Availed and Utilized ITC
explain: Merely claiming ineligible ITC does not attract interest if it remains unutilized in the credit ledger.
Interest at 18% p.a. applies only when wrongful ITC is both availed AND utilized.
ITC is treated as utilized when the ledger balance drops below the amount of wrongly availed credit.
The period of interest runs from the date of wrongful utilization until the date of reversal or payment.
To check utilization of wrong IGST credit, total balances of IGST, CGST, and SGST are evaluated together.
Compensation cess credit cannot be clubbed with IGST/CGST/SGST balances to determine utilization.

flow.title: Testing Wrong ITC Availment for Interest
steps: Wrong ITC is credited to ledger
Check if total ECL balance falls below wrong ITC
If balance never falls below, no interest applies
If balance drops, calculate shortfall as utilized
Charge 18% interest from utilization to reversal

topics.example: Zen Ltd mistakenly claimed ₹1,00,000 IGST credit in April and reversed it in July; since its total credit ledger balance stayed above ₹1,50,000 throughout, zero interest is charged.
remember: No interest is payable if wrongly availed ITC is not utilized; rate is 18% p.a. upon actual utilization.
mistakes: Levying interest on wrong ITC when the taxpayer's credit ledger balance never dipped below the wrong credit amount.

quiz.q: Under Section 50(3), interest is attracted on input tax credit when it is:
quiz.why: Section 50(3) explicitly requires that input tax credit must be both wrongly availed and utilized to attract interest.

quiz.q: For calculating interest on wrongly availed IGST credit, which balances in the credit ledger are considered together?
o: Total ITC of IGST, CGST, and SGST
Electronic Cash Ledger and Credit Ledger
quiz.why: Circular No. 192/04/2023 clarifies that total ITC under IGST, CGST, and SGST taken together is considered.

topics.title: Transfer of Input Tax Credit between Governments
topics.section: Section 53, 53A of CGST Act & Section 17A, 18 of IGST Act
explain: When CGST credit is utilized to pay IGST, the Central Government transfers that sum from CGST to IGST account.
When IGST credit is utilized to pay CGST/UTGST, funds move from the IGST account to the CGST/UTGST account.
When IGST credit is utilized for SGST, the Centre apportions and transfers that amount to the respective State.
'Appropriate State' refers to the State or Union Territory where the taxable person is registered.
Section 53A ensures matching inter-government revenue transfers when cash ledger balances are moved across heads.

flow.title: Inter-Government Credit Settlement
steps: Taxpayer utilizes credit of one tax for another
Source tax collection is reduced accordingly
Central Government identifies destination head
Funds transferred from source to destination treasury

topics.example: A firm in Tamil Nadu uses ₹15,000 of its IGST credit to clear its SGST liability; the Central Government transfers ₹15,000 from the IGST account to Tamil Nadu's State account.
remember: Government handles revenue transfers between CGST, IGST, and SGST automatically based on return filings.
mistakes: Assuming the taxpayer has to manually remit funds to the State Government when using IGST credit for SGST.

quiz.q: When CGST credit is utilized for payment of IGST dues, which transfer is made by the Central Government?
o: Transfer from SGST to IGST account
Transfer from CGST account to IGST account
Transfer from IGST account to CGST account
Transfer from Central Government to State Government
quiz.why: Under Section 53 of the CGST Act, an amount equal to the CGST credit utilized is transferred from the CGST account to the IGST account.

quiz.q: Where IGST credit is used to discharge SGST liability, to whom does the Central Government transfer the equivalent amount?
quiz.why: Section 18 of the IGST Act provides that the amount is transferred to the account of the appropriate State Government.
